items.prompt: Which scale do geologists use to rank the hardness of minerals?

options.label: Mohs scale
Kelvin scale
Richter scale
Beaufort scale

rubric: The Mohs scale ranks minerals from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond) by scratch resistance.
Richter measures earthquakes, which is a common mix-up.

items.prompt: Which rock type forms when molten rock cools and solidifies?

options.label: Sedimentary
Clastic
Metamorphic
Igneous

rubric: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma or lava.
Sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form by other processes.

items.prompt: What is the name of a plate boundary where two plates move apart from each other?

options.label: Conformable
Convergent
Transform
Divergent

rubric: Divergent boundaries are where plates separate, such as mid-ocean ridges.
Convergent means plates move together; transform means they slide past each other.

items.prompt: Which instrument records the waves released by an earthquake?

options.label: Anemometer
Barometer
Spectrometer
Seismograph

rubric: A seismograph records ground motion from seismic waves.
The other instruments measure pressure, wind speed and light.

items.prompt: Which layer of the Earth is made of liquid metal?

options.label: Outer core
Crust
Mantle
Inner core

rubric: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel.
The inner core is solid because of the extreme pressure; the mantle is mostly solid rock.

items.prompt: Which of the following are minerals rather than rocks? Select all that apply.

options.label: Calcite
Sandstone
Granite
Quartz
Feldspar

rubric: Quartz, feldspar and calcite are single minerals with defined compositions.
Granite and sandstone are rocks made of several minerals or grains.

items.prompt: A hiker on a volcano sees glowing molten rock flowing across the ground surface from a vent. Geologists use different words for molten rock depending on where it is. What is the correct term for this molten rock once it has reached the surface?

options.label: Tephra
Lava
Ash
Magma

rubric: Molten rock is called lava once it erupts at the surface.
Magma is the term for molten rock underground.

items.prompt: Why are fossils found mostly in sedimentary rocks rather than igneous rocks?

options.label: Sedimentary rocks are always older than igneous rocks, so they hold more ancient life
Sediment buries remains gently at low temperature; molten rock destroys them
Igneous rocks form too deep underground for any living thing to ever reach them
Sedimentary rocks contain dissolved minerals that slowly turn buried remains into bone

rubric: Burial in sediment preserves organisms; the heat of magma or lava destroys them.
Age and depth are not the reason, and minerals do not create bones.

items.prompt: Limestone is buried deep and subjected to heat and pressure without melting. What most likely happens to it?

options.label: It melts and cools to form basalt
It recrystallises into marble, a metamorphic rock
It breaks into sand and becomes sandstone
It stays unchanged because pressure cannot affect rock

rubric: Heat and pressure without melting causes metamorphism; limestone becomes marble.
Melting would produce igneous rock, which is the common misconception here.

items.prompt: Why do most earthquakes happen near plate boundaries?

options.label: Plate boundaries are where the crust is thinnest and weakest to rain
Plates snag as they move, then release stored stress by slipping
Gravity is stronger at boundaries, which pulls rock downward suddenly
Magma underneath the boundaries pushes upward and cracks the surface

rubric: Stress builds where plates lock together, then releases as seismic waves when they slip.
Magma and gravity explanations confuse earthquakes with volcanism.

items.prompt: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and forms a cave. How is this process classified?

options.label: Mechanical weathering
Deposition
Chemical weathering
Erosion

rubric: Dissolving rock through a chemical reaction with water is chemical weathering.
Erosion involves transport, and mechanical weathering involves physical breakage without changing chemistry.

items.prompt: A cliff shows horizontal sedimentary layers that have never been folded or flipped. Which statement about their ages is correct?

options.label: The top layer is oldest because it has been exposed to weathering the longest
The thickest layer is oldest because it took the longest to form
All layers are the same age because they formed together
The bottom layer is oldest because layers were deposited on top of it

rubric: By the law of superposition, undisturbed layers get younger upward.
Surface exposure and thickness do not indicate age.

items.prompt: Which observations support the theory of plate tectonics? Select all that apply.

options.label: The continents have stayed in fixed positions throughout Earth's history
The same fossil species appear on continents now separated by oceans
Earthquakes and volcanoes cluster in belts along plate edges
The coasts of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces
Seafloor rock is oldest at the mid-ocean ridges

rubric: Coastline fit, shared fossils and earthquake and volcano belts all support moving plates.
Seafloor is youngest at ridges, and fixed continents contradict the theory.

items.prompt: A student compares two igneous rocks. Granite has large, visible crystals, while basalt from a lava flow has crystals too small to see. The student wants to explain the difference. Which explanation is best?

options.label: Basalt was exposed to water, which dissolved its large crystals
Granite contains denser minerals, so its crystals grow larger than basalt's
Granite cooled slowly underground, letting crystals grow large
Basalt cooled slowly at the surface, which kept its crystals tiny

rubric: Slow cooling at depth allows large crystals; fast surface cooling gives small ones.
The reversed cooling-rate distractor is the common misconception.

items.prompt: A rock has large, visible, interlocking crystals of quartz and feldspar. What does this texture most likely tell you about how it formed?

options.label: Magma cooled slowly deep underground, giving crystals time to grow
Lava cooled quickly at the surface, so crystals grew large
Sediment grains were pressed and cemented together over time
Heat and pressure recrystallized an older rock without melting it

rubric: Large crystals form when magma cools slowly at depth.
Distractors confuse the texture with extrusive, sedimentary or metamorphic origins.

items.prompt: Basalt from a lava flow is fine-grained, with crystals too small to see. Why?

options.label: It was squeezed under such high pressure that its crystals were crushed small
The lava cooled quickly at the surface, leaving little time for crystals
It was buried deep and cooled slowly, so crystals stayed small under pressure
It was cemented from tiny mineral grains deposited in a riverbed or lake

rubric: Rapid cooling at the surface gives small crystals.
Distractors link small grains to burial, sediments or crushing.

items.prompt: Marble is made of interlocking calcite crystals and was once limestone. How is marble classified?

options.label: Sedimentary, because it began as limestone and still has that composition
Volcanic, because it formed from cooled lava at the surface
Igneous, because its interlocking crystals show it cooled from a melt
Metamorphic, because heat and pressure changed the original rock

rubric: Marble is limestone recrystallized by heat and pressure.
The sedimentary distractor ignores that the rock has changed; the igneous one mistakes crystal texture for melting.

items.prompt: At a boundary where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the oceanic plate sinks beneath the continent. Why does the oceanic plate sink?

options.label: It is thinner, so the continent pushes it down
It is denser than continental crust
It is hotter, so it melts at the surface
It moves faster, so it dives under the slower plate

rubric: Oceanic crust is denser and so subducts.
Distractors cite thickness, heat or speed rather than density.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of erosion rather than weathering?

options.label: Tree roots pry apart a rock ledge
Acid rain slowly dissolves the surface of a limestone statue
Frost wedging splits a boulder along a crack
A river carries sand from a hillside to a delta

rubric: Erosion is the transport of material; weathering breaks it down in place.
The other options are all breakdown processes with no transport.

items.prompt: Which of the following rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies? Select all that apply.

options.label: Marble
Sandstone
Obsidian
Basalt
Granite

rubric: Granite, basalt and obsidian form from cooled magma or lava.
Sandstone is sedimentary and marble is metamorphic.

items.prompt: A hiker finds layered sandstone containing fossil seashells near the top of a high mountain, far from any ocean. A friend asks how marine fossils got there. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: The sediments were laid down in a sea, then lifted by tectonic forces
Volcanic eruptions blasted marine sediment and shells up to the summit
Strong winds carried the shells inland from the coast and buried them
Sea level once rose high enough to cover the mountain, then fell back

rubric: Marine sediments can be uplifted by tectonic collision.
Distractors invent transport or formation methods that don't fit sedimentary layers.

items.prompt: An unknown mineral scratches calcite (hardness 3) but is itself scratched by quartz (hardness 7). Using the Mohs scale, what is its hardness range?

options.label: Between 3 and 7
Less than 3
Greater than 7
Exactly 7

rubric: It is harder than 3 and softer than 7.
Other options reverse or ignore one of the scratch results.

items.prompt: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 10 million years. A rock sample has 25% of its original parent isotope left. About how old is the rock?

options.label: 20 million years
25 million years
40 million years
10 million years

rubric: 25% left means two half-lives, so 20 million years.
Distractors use one half-life, the percentage directly, or four half-lives.

items.prompt: A gray rock contains visible fragments of fossil shells and fizzes when a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid is applied. Which rock is it most likely?

options.label: Basalt
Granite
Slate
Limestone

rubric: Fizzing indicates calcite, and fossils indicate sedimentary limestone.
The others are not carbonate or fossil-bearing rocks.

items.prompt: Two plates move apart at 4 cm per year. If the rate stays constant, about how far apart will they move in 5 million years?

options.label: 200 km
20 km

rubric: Distractors come from unit conversion slips by factors of ten.

items.prompt: A quartz-rich sandstone is buried deep and subjected to high heat and pressure, without melting. What rock does it become?

options.label: Granite
Obsidian
Shale
Quartzite

rubric: Sandstone recrystallizes into metamorphic quartzite.
Distractors name igneous or sedimentary rocks, ignoring the metamorphic step in the rock cycle.

items.prompt: At a divergent boundary on the ocean floor, which features would you expect to find? Select all that apply.

options.label: A deep-ocean trench
A chain of explosive andesitic volcanoes
A mid-ocean ridge
New basaltic crust
Shallow earthquakes

rubric: Spreading centres have ridges, shallow quakes and new basalt.
Trenches and andesitic volcanic arcs belong to convergent boundaries.

items.prompt: A cross-section of a road cut shows horizontal layers of sandstone over shale. A vertical sheet of granite cuts across both layers from bottom to top. A student must decide which is younger, the granite sheet or the layers it cuts.

options.label: The granite is older, because igneous rocks form deep and are older than sedimentary rocks
The layers are younger, because the oldest rock is always found at the bottom of a section
The granite is younger, because it had to form after the rock it breaks through
They are the same age, because rocks in direct contact formed in one event

rubric: By cross-cutting relationships, a feature that cuts others is younger.
Distractors ignore the rule or assume igneous rocks are always older.

items.prompt: A volcanic island chain forms as a plate moves over a fixed hotspot. An extinct island 600 km from the active hotspot is 6 million years old. What is the plate's average speed?

options.label: 10 cm/yr
1 cm/yr
60 cm/yr
0.6 cm/yr

rubric: 600 km / 6 Myr = 100 km/Myr = 10 cm/yr.
Distractors come from unit conversion slips by a factor of 10.

items.prompt: A mineral's parent isotope has a half-life of 500 million years. A sample keeps 25% of its original parent isotope, and no daughter isotope was present at the start. How old is the sample?

options.label: 1.5 billion years
2 billion years
1 billion years
500 million years

rubric: 25% remaining is two half-lives, so 2 x 500 = 1 billion years.
Distractors confuse the percent remaining with the number of half-lives.

items.prompt: An unknown mineral scratches fluorite (hardness 4) but is scratched by apatite (hardness 5). What is its Mohs hardness?

options.label: Between 3 and 4
Between 6 and 7
Between 4 and 5
Between 5 and 6

rubric: It is harder than 4 and softer than 5.
Distractors reverse the scratch relationship.

items.prompt: In one outcrop, folded shale and limestone are cut across by a granite intrusion. The granite was then eroded, and a flat-lying conglomerate containing granite pebbles rests on it. What is the order from oldest to youngest?

options.label: Folded shale and limestone, granite, conglomerate
Folded shale and limestone, conglomerate, granite
Conglomerate, granite, folded shale and limestone
Granite, folded shale and limestone, conglomerate

rubric: The granite cuts the folded beds, so it is younger, and the conglomerate contains granite pebbles, so it is youngest.
Distractors ignore the cross-cutting and included-fragment principles.

items.prompt: A pure quartz sandstone is buried deeply, then heated and squeezed without melting. Which rock results?

options.label: Slate
Quartzite
Gneiss
Marble

rubric: Metamorphism of quartz sandstone yields quartzite.
Marble comes from limestone and slate from shale.

items.prompt: At a convergent boundary where oceanic plate subducts beneath continental plate, which features should you predict? Select all that apply.

options.label: A rift valley with fissure basalt eruptions
A volcanic arc on the continental margin
A deep ocean trench offshore
Earthquakes dipping along the subducting slab
New oceanic crust forming at the boundary

rubric: Subduction produces trenches, arc volcanoes and dipping earthquake zones.
New crust and rift valleys belong to divergent boundaries.

items.prompt: A seismology class compares a magnitude 5.0 earthquake with a magnitude 7.0 earthquake. Each whole magnitude step releases about 32 times more energy. Roughly how many times more energy does the magnitude 7.0 event release?

options.label: About 64 times, because the two steps add: 32 + 32
About 1,000 times, because the two steps multiply: 32 x 32
About 100 times, because each step is a factor of 10
About 320 times, because 32 is multiplied by 10 for the steps

rubric: Two steps give 32 x 32, about 1,000.
Distractors add the steps or assume a factor of 10 per step.

items.prompt: Two volcanoes sit in the same region: one produces fluid lava flows, the other violent ash eruptions. Which difference in magma best explains this?

options.label: The explosive volcano's magma is richer in silica, so it is more viscous and traps gas
The fluid volcano's magma is richer in silica, so it flows farther and loses gas slowly
The fluid volcano's magma holds more dissolved gas, so it pushes lava out steadily
The explosive volcano's magma is hotter, so it is thinner and releases gas violently

rubric: High silica raises viscosity and traps gas, causing explosions.
Distractors reverse the effect of silica or temperature.

items.prompt: A sandstone has angular, poorly sorted grains of quartz and feldspar in a clay-rich matrix. What does this most likely indicate about its history?

options.label: Short transport and rapid deposition, so grains were little abraded or sorted
Slow deposition on a beach, so wave action washed out the fine clay and sorted the grains
Long wind transport, so repeated grain collisions rounded and sorted the grains
Deep burial metamorphism, so the grains recrystallised into angular shapes

rubric: Angular, unsorted grains with clay indicate little transport and rapid burial.
Distractors describe processes that would round or sort grains.

items.prompt: An igneous rock has large feldspar crystals about 5 mm across set in a fine-grained groundmass. What cooling history best explains this?

options.label: Uniform rapid cooling, with large crystals growing from trapped gas bubbles
Uniform slow cooling in a deep chamber, with fine grains from added water
Rapid cooling at the surface first, then slow cooling after deep burial
Slow cooling at depth first, then faster cooling nearer the surface

rubric: Porphyritic texture records two cooling stages: slow, then fast.
Distractors give one stage or reverse the order.

items.prompt: A student finds marine fossil shells in limestone at 4,000 m elevation and concludes sea level once stood 4,000 m higher than today. Which critique is strongest?

options.label: Global sea level has been stable, so rivers must have carried the shells uphill from the coast
Limestone often forms in lakes and caves, so the shells were likely deposited by freshwater
The rock probably formed on a seafloor and was later uplifted by plate collision
Marine shells are too fragile to be preserved in limestone, so they were probably carried in by wind

rubric: Tectonic uplift explains marine rocks at height without huge sea-level change.
Distractors rest on false claims about limestone or fossils.

items.prompt: A limestone region has caves and sinkholes, while nearby granite forms rounded boulders in clay-rich soil. What best explains the contrast?

options.label: Limestone is rich in quartz, which splits along grain boundaries by frost wedging and opens caves
Granite is softer than limestone, so physical abrasion alone grinds it down into clay-rich soil
Granite is more soluble than limestone in rain, so it dissolves away and leaves rounded boulders
Calcite dissolves in slightly acidic water, while granite's feldspar slowly alters to clay

rubric: Chemical weathering dissolves calcite and converts feldspar to clay.
Distractors misstate hardness, composition or solubility.

items.prompt: Which observations support seafloor spreading at a mid-ocean ridge? Select all that apply.

options.label: Seafloor rock is oldest at the ridge crest
Magnetic stripes mirror each other across the ridge
Seafloor rock gets older with distance from the ridge crest
Heat flow is lowest at the ridge crest
Sediment gets thicker with distance from the ridge crest

rubric: Symmetric stripes, increasing age and thickening sediment all fit new crust forming at the ridge.
The ridge crest is youngest and hottest, so the last two are reversed.

items.prompt: Mapping a ridge, a field team finds the oldest rocks (Cambrian) along the crest, with progressively younger Ordovician and Silurian beds on both flanks, each dipping away from the crest. What structure is this, and what force formed it?

options.label: A syncline, formed by compressional folding
An anticline, formed by compressional folding
A graben, formed by tensional faulting
A horst, formed by tensional block faulting

rubric: Oldest beds in the core dipping away indicate an anticline, formed by compression.
A syncline has youngest beds in the core; horsts and grabens are fault blocks.

items.prompt: A road cut shows a granite body with a thin, fine-grained rim against the surrounding limestone, and the limestone next to the contact has recrystallised to marble for about 2 m. What does the fine-grained rim of the granite most directly indicate?

options.label: Faster cooling of the magma against cooler country rock at the contact
Slower cooling at the margin because the limestone insulated the magma
Weathering of the granite rim by groundwater moving along the contact
Metamorphism of the granite by later regional pressure

rubric: A chilled margin forms where magma loses heat quickly to cold host rock, giving small crystals.
Distractors reverse the cooling logic or invoke later processes that would not produce a thin rim.

items.prompt: On a geologic map, a sequence of sedimentary layers is cut by a granite pluton, and the pluton is itself overlain by a flat sandstone unit that contains granite pebbles at its base. What is the correct order of events from oldest to youngest?

options.label: Flat sandstone deposition, layered sediments, granite intrusion, erosion
Layered sediments, granite intrusion, uplift and erosion, flat sandstone deposition
Granite intrusion, layered sediments, erosion, flat sandstone deposition
Layered sediments, flat sandstone deposition, granite intrusion, uplift and erosion

rubric: Cross-cutting shows the granite is younger than the layers it cuts; granite pebbles in the sandstone show the granite was exposed and eroded first.
Distractors ignore the cross-cutting rule or the significance of the included pebbles.

items.prompt: A volcano repeatedly produces violent explosive eruptions with ash columns, while a nearby volcano on the same plate boundary mostly oozes lava flows. Both have similar mantle sources. Which difference best explains the contrast?

options.label: The explosive volcano has silica-rich, gas-charged magma that is viscous and traps gas
The explosive volcano has silica-poor, runny magma, so gas escapes slowly and builds up pressure
The explosive volcano sits closer to the trench, so seawater contact makes all its eruptions explosive
The explosive volcano is older, so its magma chamber is hotter and its magma more fluid and gas-rich

rubric: Viscous, silica-rich magma traps gas and fragments explosively.
Distractors reverse the viscosity relationship or invoke location or age as a direct cause.

items.prompt: Seismograph stations record an earthquake. Station A detects the S-P arrival gap of 30 s, station B 60 s, and station C 45 s. Which conclusion follows about the epicentre?

options.label: One station's gap fixes the epicentre's exact direction, so a second station only confirms the bearing
Station B is farthest, and three stations' distances locate it by intersecting circles
Station B is closest, because a longer gap means stronger shaking and a larger recorded amplitude
Station A is farthest, because S waves arrive later at nearer stations, which shortens the gap there

rubric: A larger S-P gap means greater distance; three distances triangulate the location.
Distractors confuse gap with amplitude or think one station gives direction.

items.prompt: A sandstone cliff shows bedding that is steeply tilted, topped by a flat-lying conglomerate with a sharp, erosional lower surface. What does this contact represent?

options.label: A cross-cutting igneous intrusion that baked and flattened the overlying unit
A fault contact, since the bedding angle differs sharply across the surface
An angular unconformity recording tilting and erosion before renewed deposition
A conformity, since the conglomerate was laid down on the sandstone without a break

rubric: Tilted beds truncated by flat beds mark a gap in time: deformation then erosion then deposition.
Distractors treat the contact as continuous, faulted or intrusive without evidence.

items.prompt: A geologist finds a rock with interlocking coarse crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica showing parallel banding. Which observations support classifying it as a metamorphic gneiss rather than an igneous granite? Select all that apply.

options.label: Minerals aligned into distinct light and dark bands
Foliation that runs parallel across the outcrop
Coarse crystals alone, since only granite can be coarse
Absence of fossils, since only sedimentary-derived gneiss lacks them

rubric: Banding and foliation reflect directed pressure and metamorphism.
Coarse crystals occur in both rocks; absence of fossils does not distinguish them.

items.prompt: A hiker finds a valley with a U-shaped cross-profile, striations on bedrock, and scattered boulders of a rock type found only 40 km up-valley. A nearby V-shaped valley lacks these features. Which process best explains the U-shaped valley and boulders?

options.label: Glacial erosion and transport of rock that was later deposited as the ice melted
Tectonic folding that formed a U shape and raised foreign boulders
Wind abrasion that sculpted a U shape and moved the boulders
River downcutting that widened the valley and carried boulders in floods only

rubric: U-shaped profiles, striations and erratics are diagnostic of glaciation.
Distractors assign glacial signatures to rivers, wind or folding.

items.prompt: A town must choose a building site near an active fault. Criteria: minimise ground-shaking amplification and liquefaction risk. Which site is best?

options.label: Water-saturated loose sand beside a river, 5 km from the fault
Bedrock outcrop on a hill, 5 km from the fault
Soft clay-filled basin, 5 km from the fault
Reclaimed fill along a harbour, 3 km from the fault

rubric: Solid bedrock reduces amplification and has no liquefaction risk.
Distractors are soft or saturated sediments that amplify shaking or liquefy.

items.prompt: A student claims that all the rocks on the seafloor are older than continental rocks because oceans are older features. Which critique is best supported by evidence?

options.label: The claim is correct, because continents grew outward from the seafloor over time and so formed later than it
The claim is correct, because seafloor crust is never destroyed and so keeps accumulating
Seafloor crust is young, since subduction recycles it, so the oldest rocks are on continents
The claim fails, because continental rocks are continuously replaced at ridges while seafloor stays put

rubric: Oceanic crust is subducted and is mostly under about 200 million years old; continents hold much older rocks.
Distractors misplace where crust is created and destroyed.

items.prompt: A quarry needs a rock for a coastal sea wall. Criteria: resists abrasion, low porosity, and does not dissolve in slightly acidic seawater. Which rock is the best choice?

options.label: Dense granite
Poorly cemented sandstone
Limestone
Shale

rubric: Granite is hard, low in porosity and chemically resistant.
Limestone dissolves in acid, shale splits easily, loose sandstone is porous and weak.

items.prompt: Two hypotheses explain a chain of islands that gets progressively older in one direction: a mantle hotspot under a moving plate, or a transform fault. Given the criterion that the explanation must account for volcanic age progression, which is better supported?

options.label: Either equally, since both produce sequential volcanism along a line
Hotspot, since the plate moves over a fixed magma source
Neither, since age progression is produced by sea-level change
Transform fault, since lateral slip steadily melts rock along the fault line

rubric: A fixed hotspot explains age progression along the plate motion direction.
Transform faults do not generally generate volcanism or age tracks.

items.prompt: To date a lava flow that is 2 million years old, which method is most appropriate given the criteria of a suitable half-life and a datable igneous mineral?

options.label: Counting tree rings in the flow
Potassium-argon dating of the volcanic minerals
Carbon-14 dating of the basalt
Measuring the thickness of weathering rind alone

rubric: K-Ar has a half-life suited to million-year-old volcanic rock.
Carbon-14 is too short-lived and needs organic material; the others are imprecise or irrelevant.

items.prompt: A planner ranks hazards for a town beside a stratovolcano. Criteria: the hazard must be capable of killing many people with little warning. Which hazards best meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Slow lava flows on gentle slopes
Pyroclastic density currents
Minor ashfall of a few millimetres
Lahars on river valleys

rubric: Pyroclastic flows and lahars are fast and deadly.
Slow lava flows and thin ashfall allow evacuation and cause fewer deaths.

items.prompt: A consultant argues a hillside is stable because it has been intact for 200 years. The slope is steep, made of weathered clay over smooth bedrock dipping out of the slope, and the region is expecting heavier rainfall. Which critique of the consultant's reasoning is best?

options.label: The argument is sound, because a slope that has survived 200 years has outlasted any plausible landslide recurrence interval
The argument is sound, because bedrock dipping out of the slope is smooth and so adds no driving force to the clay above it
The argument fails mainly because clay is a strong, cohesive material that heavy rain makes more stable
Past stability is weak evidence, since rain-saturated clay on a dipping smooth surface can fail suddenly

rubric: Failure planes and increased pore pressure make failure likely even after long stability.
Distractors treat history as proof or ignore bedding orientation.

items.prompt: A granite body contains angular blocks of the schist that surrounds it, and the schist shows a baked, recrystallised zone along the contact. Which conclusion is best supported by this evidence?

options.label: The granite is older, because pieces of one rock found inside another must have come from the older rock that hosts them
The granite intruded after the schist formed, because the blocks were broken off and the contact was heated
The schist formed after the granite, because it wraps around the granite and so must have been deposited on it later
Both formed together, because the baked contact shows the two rocks were metamorphosed at the same time under one event

rubric: Inclusions of the host plus a contact aureole show the granite intruded the schist, so it is younger (inclusion and baked-contact principles).
Distractors misapply 'wrapping' or 'fragments' logic without noting that the fragments are of the host, not of the granite.

items.prompt: A K-Ar date on biotite from a gneiss gives 180 Ma, but zircon U-Pb in the same rock gives 1.1 Ga. Judging by closure-temperature behaviour, which critique of reading 180 Ma as the rock's formation age is strongest?

options.label: Zircon U-Pb ages are unreliable in gneiss because zircon grows only during weathering, so the K-Ar age is the real one
Argon escaped biotite during later reheating, so 180 Ma records cooling below its closure temperature
K-Ar ages are always younger than U-Pb because potassium-40 decays faster than uranium in every mineral
Biotite is too small a mineral to retain potassium, so the K-Ar result reflects analytical noise rather than any geologic event

rubric: Argon is lost above biotite's closure temperature, so the K-Ar date records cooling or reheating, while zircon preserves the crystallisation age.
Distractors invent decay-rate or grain-size explanations instead of closure-temperature resetting.

items.prompt: A seismologist must decide whether a belt of earthquakes marks a subduction zone or a transform boundary. Which single observation best discriminates between the two?

options.label: The belt lies near a coastline, which is where subduction zones occur and transform faults never do
Most events have magnitudes below 5, which indicates a boundary where plates slide past each other sideways
Hypocentres deepen along a plane dipping beneath the overriding plate to several hundred kilometres depth
Earthquakes occur in a narrow linear band at the surface, which only a transform fault can produce

rubric: A dipping Wadati-Benioff zone of deepening hypocentres is diagnostic of subduction; transforms have shallow seismicity.
Distractors use magnitude, linearity or coastal position, none of which separates the boundary types.

items.prompt: A student argues that a sandstone with well-rounded, frosted quartz grains must have been deposited close to its source because 'the grains look fresh and clean'. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Strong rounding and frosting of hard quartz usually record long transport or recycling, so the inference is reversed
The argument is correct because quartz is a soft mineral that rounds within a few metres of transport from its source rock
Rounding is produced mainly by chemical weathering in the source area, so it says little about how far the grains were carried by water or wind
Frosting is produced by glacial grinding, and glacial transport usually moves grains only short distances from bedrock outcrops, so the source is close

rubric: Quartz is hard, so strong rounding implies long or repeated transport (textural maturity), the opposite of the student's claim.
Distractors misattribute rounding to chemistry, glaciers or softness.

items.prompt: A town sits 45 km down a river valley from a glacier-capped stratovolcano. Criteria: highest likelihood of killing people with minutes of warning, and reach beyond the volcano's flanks. Which hazard should be ranked first for evacuation planning?

options.label: Volcanic gas emissions, since dense gases can pool in valleys and suffocate people far from the vent
Ballistic blocks, since they are thrown at high speed and can strike people at distances of many kilometres
Lahars channelled down the valley, since melted ice and ash can reach the town quickly with little warning
Lava flows, since they are the most common eruptive product and often extend far down valleys from stratovolcanoes

rubric: Lahars from ice melt travel tens of kilometres down valleys fast with little warning, fitting both criteria.
Distractors name hazards that are usually local to the flanks (lava, ballistics) or overstate gas uniformity.

items.prompt: A researcher claims a large asteroid impact caused a mass extinction recorded in a thin clay layer. Which observations would most strongly support an impact origin of that layer? Select all that apply.

options.label: Fossils of many species found only in the beds below the layer
A local sandstone bed that thickens toward a nearby river channel
A worldwide iridium enrichment in the layer far above normal crustal levels
Shocked quartz grains with intersecting planar deformation features
Glassy spherules that formed from ejected melt and fell out globally

rubric: Global iridium, shocked quartz and impact spherules are characteristic impact signatures that are hard to explain by ordinary processes.
Fossils below the layer or a local channel sandstone say nothing about the cause of the boundary.

items.prompt: A geologist maps tilted sandstone (A) and shale (B) cut by a normal fault. Above an angular unconformity lies flat conglomerate (C), which is not offset by the fault. Boulders in C include fragments of A and B. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.label: The fault formed after A and B were tilted and C was deposited, then C was later eroded to look unfaulted
The fault is younger than A and B but older than C, which was deposited after tilting, faulting and erosion
C is older than A and B because conglomerate always forms before sandstone and shale in a sequence
The fault is younger than C because faults always cut the youngest unit last and the offset has been eroded

rubric: The fault cuts A and B but not C, and C contains their clasts above an unconformity, so the fault predates C and postdates A and B.
Distractors reverse cross-cutting logic or assume fixed rock-type ordering.

items.prompt: You must date a fossil-bearing mudstone with the tightest possible age bracket. Constraints: absolute ages needed, no datable minerals in the mudstone, volcanic ash layers exist 2 m above and 3 m below it. Which plan fits?

options.label: Date the mudstone directly by K-Ar on its clay minerals, which record the original deposition age
Date zircons by U-Pb from both ash layers so the fossil bed is bracketed between two ages
Sample only the upper ash, because one age above the fossils is enough to bracket the bed in time
Run radiocarbon on the mudstone's carbonate, since it works for any rock older than a million years

rubric: U-Pb on zircon from ash above and below gives maximum and minimum ages for the bed.
Radiocarbon is limited to about 50,000 years, clay K-Ar is unreliable for depositional age, and one ash gives only a limit.

items.prompt: Design a field test to locate and date the most recent rupture of a fault whose trace is buried under flat alluvium. Constraints: the surface shows only a faint scarp, and you need both fault geometry and timing. Which plan meets both?

options.label: Excavate a trench across the scarp, log offset layers and date organic material above and below the break
Collect surface cobbles along the scarp and measure their hardness to estimate when the fault last moved
Map the scarp's colour changes from aerial photos and infer rupture dates from vegetation type
Drill a single vertical borehole beside the scarp and date its core to find the fault location

rubric: A trench across the scarp exposes displaced strata for geometry, and dating material above and below the break bounds the rupture time.
Other options give neither geometry nor a reliable age.

items.prompt: An agency proposes monitoring a restless volcano with seismometers alone. The goal is to tell magma moving upward from ordinary tectonic faulting. Which addition would best complete the design?

options.label: A second set of seismometers of the same type placed in the same valley to double the event count
Rock hardness tests on old lava flows to calibrate how strong the eruption might be
A weather station to track rainfall, since rain changes seismic rates more than magma does
Ground deformation (GPS or InSAR) and gas flux measurements to detect inflation and magmatic degassing

rubric: Deformation and gas data independently reveal magma intrusion, helping separate it from tectonic earthquakes.
The distractors repeat the same data type or add irrelevant measurements.

items.prompt: You need a proxy design from a 1-million-year marine sediment core to separate past ocean temperature from global ice volume. Which design meets this constraint?

options.label: Measure Mg/Ca and oxygen isotopes on the same foraminifera, then subtract the temperature effect
Measure oxygen isotopes on foraminifera from many depths, since ice volume alone controls the signal over 1 million years
Count foraminifera shells per gram, since abundance alone fixes both temperature and ice volume
Measure grain size alone, because coarse sediment always indicates a warmer ocean

rubric: Mg/Ca gives temperature, so removing it from the δ18O signal leaves ice-volume and seawater effects.
Other designs use a single ambiguous variable that cannot separate the two.

items.prompt: You are writing a field key step that must separate gabbro from basalt, which have the same mineral makeup. Which criterion should the key use to fit that constraint?

options.label: Mineral content, since gabbro is rich in plagioclase and pyroxene while basalt is mostly quartz and feldspar
Grain size, with coarse visible crystals for gabbro and fine crystals for basalt
Presence of layering, since basalt forms from sedimentary deposition in water and gabbro does not
Colour alone, since gabbro is always pale and basalt is always dark in any hand sample

rubric: Both are mafic with the same minerals; grain size, set by cooling rate, distinguishes intrusive from extrusive.
Distractors rely on composition, colour or a sedimentary origin, which do not separate them.

items.prompt: You are assembling a hazard-zoning map for a coastal city near an active subduction margin. Which layers must be included to address ground shaking and flooding risk? Select all that apply.

options.label: Tsunami inundation modelled from coastal elevation
Rock colour classification of local outcrops
Mohs hardness values of building stone samples
Liquefaction susceptibility of saturated sandy soils
Mapped active fault traces with setback zones

rubric: Fault setbacks, liquefaction and tsunami inundation are the main earthquake-related hazards the map must address.
Rock colour and stone hardness do not inform seismic or tsunami risk zoning.

items.prompt: A team needs a site to store CO2 underground. Constraints: a porous reservoir rock below 800 m, a sealing layer above it, and no faults cutting the seal. Four candidate profiles are proposed. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Porous sandstone at 1,200 m beneath thick shale, in a region with no faults crossing the shale
Porous sandstone at 400 m beneath thin limestone, which is easy to drill and shallow
Sandstone at 1,200 m beneath shale cut by an active fault, since the fault helps gas spread widely
Fractured granite from the surface down to 1,500 m, since it is strong and does not compress

rubric: Deep porous sandstone under thick intact shale caprock with no faults satisfies depth, porosity and sealing constraints.
Other profiles are too shallow, lack a seal, or have faults that would leak CO2.
